title: Practice: how to turn training into skill November 4, 2026
author: Unlocked Graduates
summary: Unlocked Graduates argues that deliberate practice should be a normal part of training and developing prison officers, because some skills cannot be learned from theory and must be rehearsed before they are needed under stress. The piece defines practice as rehearsing a skill with clear intent and improving through feedback and re-runs, and it warns that practice makes permanent rather than perfect, so rehearsal without feedback entrenches bad habits. It points to surgeons, actors and athletes as performative professions that rehearse because the moment cannot be rerun. The authors separate individual skill practice from complex scenarios and stress that challenge must rise over time. They give a five-step set-up: choose the scenario, model it, script it, run it in pairs with roles, timings and success checks, then give fast feedback and run it again. Line managers and mentors are named as the people best placed to keep practice going beyond initial training.
points: Deliberate practice has three parts, rehearsing a skill, doing it with intent, and improving through feedback and re-runs, and without feedback it hardens errors instead of fixing them.
Practice builds muscle memory that holds when working memory is overloaded by stress or complexity, which reading about the job cannot do.
Practice differs from role play because participants rehearse being themselves in a realistic scenario rather than adopting a fake persona.
A consistent set-up of scenario, model, script, paired run and feedback with a re-run frees working memory so participants can concentrate on the skill itself.
Line managers and mentors are the leverage point for sustaining practice after initial training, for example by rehearsing a difficult conversation before it happens.
quotes: The well-known phrase is that practice makes perfect. In fact, practice makes permanent. Rehearse something badly, without feedback, and the bad habit sticks.
Practice builds long term muscle memory, and that matters because officers must perform well when their working memory is overloaded, in moments of extreme stress or complexity.
Role play suggests playing a “fake” role and taking on someone else’s persona. In practice, participants rehearse being themselves as prison officers.

Surgeons practise for hundreds of hours, suturing fruit before they move to human skin. They are drilled in the height of the elbow, steady breathing through the procedure, and the exact angle of the wrist.

Roles, timings and success checks are shared up front, so participants know the purpose of the activity and how to tell whether they got it right. Sharing this, and modelling the activity, frees up working memory.

One of the best things to hear is a participant stopping and saying, “I’d never say that, let me try again.” It shows they are using the time to find something that feels authentic to them and still meets the success checks for the technique.
It needs careful planning and a clear structure. But the principle is simple: if a job has to be performed, it has to be rehearsed.
